## Overview

`method = "mghs"` fits the multiple graphical horseshoe of Busatto & Stingo
(2025, *JCGS*). The sampler is adapted from the authors' code
(github.com/cbusatto/mGHS) and reproduces its draws exactly for the same
seed. Local fixes and the validation are documented in
`system.file("mghs", package = "multiGGM")`.

### Continuous shrinkage versus spike-and-slab

The G-Wishart (`"gwishart"`) and SSVS (`"ssvs"`) samplers have a binary
indicator $g_{k,ij}$ for every edge. Each draw says which edges are in each
graph, so the package can report posterior inclusion probabilities
(`pip_edges()`) and the probability that an edge is in one graph but not the
other (`pip_diff_edge()`). Groups borrow strength through an MRF prior on
those indicators.

The mGHS has **no indicators**. Each precision entry $\omega_{k,ij}$ gets a
horseshoe prior with a global scale $\tau_k$ and a local scale
$\lambda_{ij,k}$. Small entries are shrunk strongly towards zero but are
never exactly zero. Groups borrow strength through a $K \times K$
correlation matrix $R$ that correlates each edge's local scales across
groups. $R = I$ gives independent graphical horseshoes.

So for mGHS fits:

* `pip_edges()`, `pip_diff_edge()`, `edge_counts()` and the plots built on
  them stop with an error, rather than returning a number with a different
  meaning.
* Edge strength comes from the posterior of the precision matrix or partial
  correlations (`coef()`, `fitted()`, `posterior_pcor()`, `posterior_ci()`).
* Differential edges come from the posterior of the group difference
  $D_{ij} = \rho_{1,ij} - \rho_{2,ij}$ (`diff_summary()`,
  `select_diff_edges()`).

## Fitting

```{r fit}
library(multiGGM)
sim <- simulate_multiggm(K = 2, p = 12, n = 60, perturb_prob = 0.2, seed = 1)

fit <- multiggm_mcmc(data_list = sim$data_list, method = "mghs",
                     burnin = 500, nsave = 500, seed = 1)
fit
summary(fit)
```

The trace of $R_{12}$ replaces the $\theta$ trace of the MRF samplers:

```{r trace}
plot_trace(fit, "theta")
```

## Differential edges and Bayesian FDR

`diff_summary()` gives one row per edge: the posterior mean and standard
deviation of $D$, a credible interval, and $P(|D| > c)$ for each threshold
$c$.

```{r diff-summary}
ds <- diff_summary(fit, scale = "pcor", deltas = c(0.05, 0.1))
head(ds[order(-ds$p_exceed_0.1), ])
```

`select_diff_edges()` selects the largest set of edges whose posterior
expected false discovery rate is at most `alpha`:

```{r select}
sel <- select_diff_edges(fit, alpha = 0.05, delta = 0.1)
sel
```

### Calibration caveat: do not use "the interval excludes zero"

It is tempting to call an edge differential when its credible interval for
$D$ excludes zero, i.e. to run Bayesian FDR on
$\max\{P(D > 0), P(D < 0)\}$ (the `p_sign` column). **Under a continuous
prior this is badly anti-conservative.** $P(D = 0) = 0$, so `p_sign` is not
the probability that the edge differs. An edge with the *same* true value in
both groups still has an estimated $D$ of sampling-noise size, and with large
$n$ its posterior is concentrated enough to give `p_sign` near 1. In a
simulation with p = 100 and n = 1000 per group, Bayesian FDR on `p_sign`
gave an achieved FDR of about 0.50 at a nominal 0.05; the false calls were
edges with identical true values whose $|D|$ was about 0.04 to 0.08.

The same applies to the SSVS sampler (its spike is a normal distribution)
and to G-Wishart edges present in both groups.

Use $P(|D| > \delta)$ with a $\delta$ that is meaningful for your problem.
The FDR is then controlled for the hypothesis $|D_{ij}| > \delta$: a true
difference smaller than $\delta$ counts as a null. For the indicator-based
samplers, `rule = "structural"` ($P(g_{1,ij} \ne g_{2,ij})$) is also
available.

## Memory, thinning and summary-only fits

Saved draws take $8 p^2 K \cdot$ `nsave` bytes per chain: 160 MB at
p = 100, K = 2 and 1000 draws. Two ways to reduce this:

* `thin`: the sampler runs every iteration but saves every `thin`-th draw.
* `save_draws = FALSE`: no draws are kept. The sampler keeps running sums
  over **every** post-burn-in iteration of the posterior means and of
  $D$ (mean, SD, $P(D > 0)$, $P(D < 0)$ and $P(|D| > c)$ for the thresholds
  in `diff_deltas`). `coef()`, `fitted()`, `diff_summary()` and
  `select_diff_edges()` use these; credible intervals and other draw-based
  functions are unavailable.

```{r lean}
lean <- multiggm_mcmc(data_list = sim$data_list, method = "mghs",
                      burnin = 500, nsave = 500, nchains = 2, seed = 2,
                      save_draws = FALSE, diff_deltas = c(0.05, 0.1))
select_diff_edges(lean, alpha = 0.05, delta = 0.1)
```

Chains are pooled by default in `diff_summary()` and `select_diff_edges()`.

## Stuck chains and run time

The sampler inherits a guard from the authors' code: if a local-scale
update would use parameters above $10^6$, the chain is declared stuck. This
happens when the global scale $\tau_k$ collapses or $R$ approaches a
singular matrix, and it is more frequent for small, sparse problems. With
p = 12 and n = 150 per group, 5 of 6 chains got stuck within 2,000
iterations, in both the authors' code and this package. With n = 50, none
of 6 did, and in a simulation study at p = 100 and n = 1000 all 100 fits
completed, some after a restart. The package also checks every scale draw for
non-finite values and caps every rejection loop, so a chain can no longer
hang. A stuck chain is restarted from scratch (up to `max_attempts`,
default 3) and the number of attempts is reported in `summary()`. If all
attempts fail, `multiggm_mcmc()` stops with an error.

Run time per iteration depends strongly on the data, not only on $p$: in
our runs it ranged from about 10 to over 100 ms per iteration for
$p \le 50$.
